title: Greater than whatever you are thinking of right now
subtitle: Al-Kabir: the Great, behind every Allahu Akbar you say
intro: Al-Kabir (الْكَبِيرُ) means The Great, the Most Great: Allah is greater in His essence, attributes and actions than anything that exists or can be imagined, and everything shrinks beside Him. It is the name behind Allahu Akbar, said dozens of times a day. Knowing it turns those words from habit into a reset of everything in your heart.

root.sense: Kabura means to be large, great or senior. Akbar is the comparative form: greater. Allahu Akbar does not say what Allah is greater than, so it compares Him with everything at once: your boss, your fear, your success, the universe. Al-Kabir is the One beside whom all of it is small.

key.label: What fills your field of view

knowing: Al-Kabir means He is great in every sense: {idea}great in His being, beyond any limit; great in His attributes, each one perfect; great in His deeds, so nothing is hard for Him. Everything that seems large is small beside Him{/idea}. The phrase Allahu Akbar is usually translated God is the greatest, but literally it says God is greater. Greater than what? It does not say, which means greater than anything at all.

Near names each add a shade. Al-Azim is the tremendous weight and magnitude of His greatness. Al-Mutakabbir is the claim to grandeur that belongs to Him alone. Al-Kabir is greatness as comparison: whatever you set beside Him is smaller. The Quran pairs it with Al-Aliyy, the Most High, in 22:62, 31:30, 34:23 and 40:12, and with Al-Muta'ali in 13:9.

Because He is the Great, {trap}anything we treat as bigger than Him becomes a false god{/trap}: wealth we cannot give up, people we cannot displease, desires we cannot say no to. Takbir pulls them back to their true size.
seeing: Listen to where Islam places takbir. The call to prayer opens with it: drop everything, the Greatest is calling you. If an important person knocked on your door you would leave your meal; Allahu Akbar asks for the same reflex for prayer. Prayer begins with it, and every movement is marked by it.

It also comes right after acts of worship. At the end of Ramadan the Quran asks believers to glorify Allah for having guided them (2:185); on the days of sacrifice the same instruction appears (22:37). Why takbir just when you have done something good? Because that is when a quiet pride whispers that you did well. {idea}Allahu Akbar answers: He is greater than my fast, greater than my sacrifice, greater than anything I offered.{/idea} The believers give what they give with hearts trembling that they will return to their Lord (23:60).
And Surah al-Isra ends with the command: praise Allah, who has no son, no partner in His dominion, no protector out of weakness, and declare His greatness fully (17:111).
trusting: Fear works by making something look huge: a diagnosis, a court letter, a powerful person who dislikes you. {reward}Every Allahu Akbar is a chance to put that thing back next to Al-Kabir and watch it shrink.{/reward} The danger may still be real, but it is not the biggest thing in your life. He is, and He is on the side of those who turn to Him.
The same works in good times. A promotion, a big win, praise from others: say Allahu Akbar and you protect your heart from swelling. {trap}Pride is just forgetting that Allah is greater.{/trap}
loving: There is something freeing in belonging to Someone greater than everything you fear. You never have to be the biggest presence in your own life. {reward}The heart loves Al-Kabir because His greatness is a shelter: whatever towers over you, He towers over it.{/reward}
now: The adhan goes off on your phone while you are in the middle of a tense negotiation on a video call. You are tempted to swipe it away. {idea}Allahu Akbar: the One calling you is greater than this deal.{/idea} Finish your sentence, excuse yourself, and go and meet Him.
old: Some things in my life feel bigger than anything else.
new: Allah is greater, Al-Kabir, so every fear and every success has a smaller, truer size.
try: Each time you hear Allahu Akbar today, in the adhan or your own prayer, name in your heart one specific thing He is greater than.

dua.text: Ya Kabir, You are greater than all I fear and all I chase. Make every Allahu Akbar I say true in my heart, shrink my pride and my worries before You, and let nothing in my life be bigger than You.
dua.note: Call on Al-Kabir in moments of fear or success, and fulfil the command of 17:111 to declare His greatness fully.

pairs.why: Paired in four verses: Al-Aliyy is His height above all, Al-Kabir His greatness beside which all is small.
Joined in 13:9: the Great and the Exalted, greater than all and far above every likeness to creation.
Al-Kabir is greatness by comparison; Al-Azim is the tremendous weight and magnitude of that greatness.

faq.a: Al-Kabir means The Great or The Most Great. It describes Allah as greater in His essence, attributes and actions than anything that exists or can be imagined. It is the name behind the phrase Allahu Akbar.

faq.q: What does Allahu Akbar literally mean?
faq.a: Literally, Allah is greater. Akbar is a comparative form. Because the phrase does not say what He is greater than, it means greater than everything: every person, fear, desire and achievement. It is commonly translated God is the greatest.

faq.q: What is the difference between Al-Kabir and Al-Azim?
faq.a: Al-Kabir stresses that Allah is greater than anything He could be compared to. Al-Azim stresses the magnitude and weight of His greatness, which the mind cannot encompass. The Quran pairs Al-Kabir with Al-Aliyy and Al-Azim with Al-Aliyy.

faq.q: Why do Muslims say Allahu Akbar after worship and on Eid?
faq.a: The Quran asks believers to glorify Allah for His guidance after completing Ramadan (2:185) and at the sacrifice (22:37). Saying Allahu Akbar after a good deed reminds the heart that Allah is greater than anything we offered, and guards against pride in our worship.
